extracted.intended_audience: general readers and literary/publishing professionals interested in Mark Twain's practices and opinions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative opinions from Mark Twain (in letters and memoir) about composing and presenting humorous material: choices of illustration, lecture structure and management, publication and marketing choices, and authorial control over reproductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration tone for humorous subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not humorous pictures. No. When they are good (or bad) one's humor gets no chance to play surprises on the reader. A humorous subject illustrated seriously is all right, but a humorous artist is no fit person for such work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: avoid using overtly comic illustrations for a humorous text. Prefer serious/earnest illustrations that allow the writer's feigned seriousness and surprises to function; a comic artist can undercut the writer's intended effect. Example/anti-pattern: a funny picture that gives away a joke or turns a tragic-but-ironic fact into mere comedy (the horse-kicking example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial approval of pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Could I be allowed to sit in judgment upon the pictures before they are accepted--at least those in which Cathy may figure? This is not essential. It is but a suggestion..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: authors (especially of personal or delicate material) should review and approve illustrations, particularly those depicting important characters, to protect tone and accuracy. This is presented as a reasonable request of a publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration quality and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for publication presentation: illustrations should be competent and appropriate to the piece. They should support the text's intended tone (see 'Illustration tone' entry), and not be chosen merely for humor if that will spoil the text's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture composition: alternate fact and anecdote
rubrics_metrics.description: "first, excite the audience with a spoonful of information about Fulton, then quiet down with a barrel of illustration drawn by memory from my books--and so on and so on, all through the evening; and if you are discreet and don't tell them the illustrations don't illustrate anything, they won't notice it..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical structure for a successful public lecture: intersperse small, interesting factual 'spoonfuls' with generous anecdotal illustration to entertain and reassure the audience. Use the alternation to maintain attention and give the appearance of instruction while primarily entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecturing pace and audience management
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is my custom to keep on talking till I get the audience cowed. Sometimes it takes an hour and fifteen minutes, sometimes I can do it in an hour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: adapt the duration and pacing of a lecture to audience response; the speaker may continue until the audience is suitably subdued/engaged. This reflects prioritizing live audience control over strict time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional wording to increase attention
rubrics_metrics.description: "P.S. Mark all the advertisements 'Private and Confidential,' otherwise the people will not read them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing tip: use intriguing or exclusive phrasing on promotional materials to increase readership/attention. Short, curiosity-arousing labels can make promotional copy more likely to be read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution strategy to reach broader audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why not sell simultaneous rights, for this once, to the Ladies' Home Journal or Collier's, or both, and recoup yourself?--for I would like to get it to classes that can't afford Harper's."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing strategy: consider selling simultaneous rights or issuing lower-priced formats to reach readers who cannot afford premium magazines, thereby expanding readership and recouping costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select evocative, personally meaningful images
rubrics_metrics.description: "I hope you will reproduce the cat-pile, full page. And save the photo for me in as good condition as possible. When Susy and Clara were little tots those cats had their profoundest worship... There is no duplicate of this picture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for image selection: choose images that have strong emotional resonance or unique documentary value to the author/subject; preserve originals and reproduce significant images at appropriate scale (e.g., full-page) to maximize impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of feigned seriousness as a humorous technique
rubrics_metrics.description: "You see, the humorous writer pretends to absolute seriousness (when he knows his trade) ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing principle: effective humor often relies on assuming a tone of absolute seriousness; undermining that tone (for example by mismatched illustrations or asides that reveal the artifice) can weaken comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and bundling decisions for editions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I was going to write and ask you to melt the plates and put it out of print... But this morning I examined it without temper, and saw that if I abolished the advertisement it would be literature again. So I have done it. I have struck out 700 words and inserted 5 MS pages of new matter... I hate to have the old Adam go out any more--don't put it on the presses again, let's put the new one in place of it; and next Xmas, let us bind Adam and Eve in one cover."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial/publishing criteria: revise earlier works to remove elements that degrade literary quality (e.g., advertising copy), consider replacing earlier printings with revised text, and bundle complementary pieces in a single edition when they score off against each other so that their strengths are perceived together.
